report.summary: This is a true positive: the workstation win81 (192.168.10.5, Windows 8.1, medium criticality, on the victim LAN) is acting as a botnet client of a known attacker machine outside the network. That machine is 205.174.165.73, a Kali Linux host. In the 30 minutes either side of the alert, win81 made 130 connections to it on TCP port 8080. They came at regular intervals and nearly all looked the same: about 196 bytes sent and 128 bytes received, which is the pattern of a bot checking in with its controller (beaconing). Across those connections win81 sent about 963 KB to the attacker but received only about 14 KB, which suggests data is being uploaded. The same pattern shows up from at least four other internal hosts (192.168.10.8, .9, .14 and .15), so several machines appear to be infected. The detector scored the alert flow as botnet with probability 0.99986, and all 20 neighbouring flows between the same two hosts that I checked also scored above the threshold as botnet.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine).
192.168.10.5 is the workstation win81 (Windows 8.1 64-bit) in the victim_lan zone, medium criticality, with no listed services.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.5 made 130 connections to 205.174.165.73:8080 between 13:29 and 14:20, sending 963,307 bytes and receiving 13,931 bytes in total. The alert flow itself sent 5 packets (196 bytes) and received 4 packets (128 bytes) over about 70 ms.

Port 8080 on 205.174.165.73 received 825 connections in the ±30-minute window. Between 13:40 and 14:00 there were 328 matching flows from several internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .14, .15), nearly all about 194–198 bytes sent and 128 bytes received, repeating every few tens of seconds. Some flows were much larger uploads, such as 73,339 bytes sent from 192.168.10.8.
The detector scored the alert flow as an attack with probability 0.99986 against a threshold of 0.00024, and as botnet with probability of about 1.0.
All 20 sampled neighbouring flows between 192.168.10.5 and 205.174.165.73 scored above the threshold, every one predicted as botnet.

Regular, small, near-identical connections from several LAN hosts to one external attacker address on port 8080 match botnet command-and-control check-ins. The occasional large uploads point to tasking being carried out or data being sent out.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win81 (192.168.10.5) and run a forensic check for malware.
Block 205.174.165.73 (at least on port 8080) at the perimeter firewall.
Isolate and check the other hosts connecting to 205.174.165.73:8080 (192.168.10.8, .9, .14, .15) as likely infected.
Review the large uploads to the attacker host (about 963 KB from win81 alone) for possible data theft.

uncertainties: There are no payloads, so it is not confirmed what was in the uploads or that the traffic was HTTP; the HTTP technique (T1071.001) is inferred from the port.
The search results were cut off at 100 of 328 flows, so the full list of internal hosts talking to the attacker may be incomplete.
I only scored 20 sample flows between the two hosts, not all 130.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an FTP brute-force attack on 192.168.10.50 (web-server-16), coming in through the firewall's NAT. Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 opened 2,479 flows to this one host, and 2,478 of them went to port 21. They ran from 12:42 to 13:30. Every flow was small and looked the same, which is what an automated login-guessing tool produces. The inventory notes that 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address, so traffic from external attackers shows up under it. All 9 neighbouring flows we scored also came out as brute_force. The flow data does not show whether any login worked.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 made 2,479 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 (2,478 on port 21, 1 on port 80), between 12:42:19 and 13:30:03. That is roughly 50 connections per minute.

The alert's own flow was short and small: 11 packets out (122 bytes), 17 packets back (188 bytes), over about 9.7 seconds, with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags. Across all flows between this pair, the totals were only 297,402 bytes out and 465,584 bytes back.
Other sources also hit the same server in the window: it received 2,733 flows across 36 ports, including 146 to SSH (22) and 44 to port 139.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with FTP/21, SSH/22 and HTTP/80. It has high criticality and sits in the victim LAN.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. External attacker traffic appears under this address because of NAT.

The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.99994 and labelled it brute_force (0.999998). We scored 9 sampled neighbouring flows from the same pair, and all 9 crossed the alert threshold as brute_force with probabilities around 0.9999. The features driving the score were the same for all of them: Bwd Packet Length Mean, Bwd RST Flags and Fwd IAT Min.
Thousands of short, near-identical FTP sessions that the server ends with a reset fit automated password guessing against FTP (ATT&CK T1110.001).

recommended_actions.action: Block or rate-limit the external sources behind the firewall NAT that are reaching FTP/21 on 192.168.10.50. Use the firewall's NAT logs to find the real external IPs.

Check the FTP server's authentication logs on web-server-16 for any successful login during 12:42–13:30. Reset the credentials of any account that was targeted, and consider turning off FTP or replacing it with SFTP.
Look into the SSH traffic (port 22) and the port 139 traffic to the same host in the same window, since they may be related brute-force activity.

uncertainties: Flow records carry no payload and no FTP reply codes, so it is unknown whether any login succeeded. The small, uniform sizes of the server's replies suggest failures, but that is not proof.
Because of the NAT, the real external attacker addresses cannot be seen from the flow data.
The single port-80 flow from the same source was not examined.
No CVE lookup was done, because the FTP server software and its version are not in the inventory.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: it is part of an HTTP flood (DDoS) against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality public web server. Over about 20 minutes (18:56:31 to 19:16:10), 172.16.0.1 sent 95,143 flows to the server's port 80. That source is the firewall's inside (NAT) address and is recorded as attacker traffic entering from outside. Every neighbouring flow I scored was also flagged as ddos. There is no evidence that the flood actually took the service down.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 95,143 flows to 192.168.10.50:80 between 18:56:31 and 19:16:10. That is roughly 80 flows per second. Together they carried only 1.9 MB toward the server but 1.11 GB back from it. The alert's own flow sent 20 bytes in 8 packets and got 11,595 bytes back in 6 packets over 3.9 seconds. This pattern of tiny requests and large replies is consistent with an HTTP request flood.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. It has high criticality, sits in the victim_lan zone, and the inventory notes it as a scheduled DDoS target.

172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Outside attackers show up behind this address because of NAT, so flows from it into the victim LAN are attacker traffic.

Of the 95,415 flows reaching 192.168.10.50 in the window, 95,143 come from this single source/destination pair. Because of the NAT, I can't tell from the flow data how many outside hosts are behind it.

The detector gave the alert's flow an attack probability of 0.9999 (ddos 0.99999), far above the 0.00024 threshold. The biggest factors were the spread of reply packet sizes (Bwd Packet Length Std) and the very small request packets. I scored 11 sample flows from the same pair, and all 11 alerted as ddos with a probability of about 0.99996.

The volume, the uniform flow pattern, the attacker address behind the firewall NAT and the scheduled-target note together indicate a deliberate HTTP flood, not normal web use. The server kept sending large replies throughout, so these records don't show that it stopped serving.

recommended_actions.action: Turn on HTTP rate limiting or DDoS mitigation (for example per-client request limits or an upstream scrubbing service) for web-server-16 and its public IP 205.174.165.68.
Pull the firewall or NAT logs to find the real outside source addresses behind 172.16.0.1, and block them at the edge.
Check web-server-16's availability, response times and resource use during 18:56–19:16 to see whether the service was degraded.

uncertainties: Because of the NAT at 172.16.0.1, the flow data can't show how many outside hosts took part, so I can't confirm it was truly distributed.
There is no measurement of the server's availability or performance, so I can't tell whether the denial of service worked.
I only scored a sample of 11 neighbouring flows, not all 95,143.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an HTTP denial-of-service (DoS) flood against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality public web server. The source, 172.16.0.1, is the firewall's inside address. Traffic from external attackers is NAT'd to that address, so the flood came from outside, not from the firewall itself. Within ±30 minutes of the alert, this source sent 168,028 flows to only this one host, and 168,027 of them went to port 80. The flows totalled about 70 MB sent and 1.9 GB returned. That volume of short, repeated connections fits a flood-type HTTP DoS (Hulk or GoldenEye style) rather than Slowloris. All 20 neighbouring flows I sampled also scored as DoS attacks. The flow records don't show whether the server's service was actually degraded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 min of event 2173685, 172.16.0.1 sent 168,028 flows to one destination (192.168.10.50) on 2 ports. 168,027 went to port 80. Totals were 70,389,501 forward bytes and 1,907,676,691 backward bytes, between 13:28:26 and 14:19:49. The alerted flow itself lasted 54 ms: 8 packets / 339 bytes forward, 7 packets / 11,595 bytes backward, with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 3 RST flags.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. It has high criticality, sits in the victim_lan zone, and is noted as a DoS target.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. External attacker traffic appears under this address because of NAT.
The detector scored the alerted flow with attack probability 0.99996 and family dos (0.999999). The biggest contributor was Bwd Packet Length Std.
All 20 sampled neighbouring flows on the same source/destination pair scored above the threshold with predicted family dos. Probabilities ranged from about 0.83 to 0.999.

Roughly 168k short HTTP connections from one source to one web server in about 50 minutes looks like a high-rate HTTP flood (Hulk or GoldenEye style) rather than a slow-rate attack. This matches T1499.002 Service Exhaustion Flood.

recommended_actions.action: Put rate limiting or connection limits for HTTP/80 in front of web-server-16. Find the real external source behind the firewall NAT using the firewall's translation logs, then block it upstream.
Check web-server-16's web service logs and availability for 13:28–14:20 to see whether service was degraded.

uncertainties: The flow records can't show whether the service was degraded. The server kept sending responses, so I left the success indicator false.
Because of NAT, I can't see the true external source IP from these records.
I didn't run a CVE lookup. I have no evidence of which web server software the host runs, so no CVE could be tied to this attack.
I only scored a sample of 20 of the 168k neighbouring flows.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. It shows an internal port scan from 192.168.10.8 (win-vista, a Windows Vista workstation on the victim LAN) against 192.168.10.19 (ubuntu-14-32, an Ubuntu workstation). The alerted flow carried no payload: 2 SYN packets went out and the target answered with 2 RST packets in 0.075 ms, which means port 8333 was closed. Within ±30 minutes the same pair had 596 flows across 397 distinct ports. Over the same window the source made 9,995 flows to 495 hosts and 1,054 ports. The inventory lists no services on the target, so port 8333 is not a legitimate service there. All 10 neighbouring flows I scored were also classed as port_scan. The source is not a known attacker address, so this looks like a compromised internal host doing discovery (likely lateral-movement reconnaissance). Nothing shows the scan achieved anything.

findings.statement: The alerted flow 3105744 (192.168.10.8:59793 -> 192.168.10.19:8333/TCP) carried 0 bytes each way: 2 SYN packets out, 2 RST packets back, lasting 0.075 ms.

Within ±30 minutes, the same source-destination pair had 596 flows to 397 distinct destination ports (top ports 139, 445, 1, 12657, 24696, 137), carrying only 28,744 bytes forward and 37,896 bytes back.
Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 made 9,995 flows to 495 distinct IPs and 1,054 distinct ports.
192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in the victim_lan zone with medium criticality. It is not a known attacker address.
192.168.10.19 is ubuntu-14-32, an Ubuntu 14.04 workstation in the victim_lan zone with no services listed. Port 8333 (Bitcoin) is not a known service on it.
The detector gave the alert an attack probability of 0.99994, classed as port_scan (0.999998). The main drivers were a backward packet length mean of 0 and 2 backward RST flags.
All 10 neighbouring flows I scored from the same pair were above the threshold and classed as port_scan.

Hundreds of empty connection attempts to many ports, answered with RST, is a typical TCP port scan. Since the source is an internal workstation that is not a known attacker, it was probably compromised and is mapping the internal network. This matches T1046 Network Service Discovery.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) and run a forensic and malware triage on it. The host is scanning hundreds of internal hosts and ports, which suggests it has been compromised.
Check which hosts and ports the source reached that gave non-RST responses, especially SMB/NetBIOS ports 139 and 445, and look for any later exploitation of those services.
Find out how 192.168.10.8 was first compromised by reviewing its earlier inbound and outbound activity, including its heavy DNS and HTTPS traffic.

uncertainties: How 192.168.10.8 was first compromised has not been established from the evidence.
I only checked the target 192.168.10.19 for successful connections. The other 494 hosts the source contacted were not checked for open-port responses or later exploitation.
The predict_attack output was cut off, so not every per-flow detail was visible, although the summary says all 10 flows were above the threshold.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. It looks like a Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) memory-leak exploit against the OpenSSL service on TCP 444 of ubuntu-server-12 (192.168.10.51, high criticality). The source address 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's NAT address, and traffic from it into this network is attacker traffic. Over ±30 minutes, 19 flows went from that address to this one host, 14 of them to port 444. The server sent back about 72 MB while the source sent only about 81 KB. In the alerted flow alone, the client sent 7,920 bytes and got back 7,883,880 bytes. The asset notes say Heartbleed against port 444 on this host was scheduled. The detector labels the flow web_attack, but the traffic fits TLS heartbeat over-read better. Large server replies are consistent with memory being leaked, which suggests the exploit worked.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.51 is ubuntu-server-12, a high-criticality Ubuntu 12.04 server in the victim LAN that runs an OpenSSL service on port 444. Its asset notes say Heartbleed against port 444 on this host was scheduled.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Because of NAT, traffic from external attackers shows up with this source address.

Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 19 flows, all to 192.168.10.51, on 4 ports: 444 (14), 80 (3), 443 (1) and 0 (1). Across those flows the source sent 81,517 bytes and the server sent back 72,222,411 bytes. In the alerted flow, 2,796 forward packets carried 7,920 bytes and 2,007 backward packets carried 7,883,880 bytes, over about 119 seconds.
The detector scored the alerted flow at 0.71 attack probability, far above the 0.00024 threshold, and labelled it web_attack. The biggest driver was a high Bwd Packet Length Std (about 2,443).

All 12 neighbouring flows I scored were above the threshold. The long port-444 sessions were predicted web_attack at about 0.97–0.996 probability. Two very short flows (2241813 and 2241814) were predicted port_scan.
CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed, CVSS 7.5) lets remote attackers read process memory through crafted TLS heartbeat packets in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1g.

Small repeated client requests drawing very large server replies from an OpenSSL service fit Heartbleed memory over-reads (exploitation of an exposed service). The detector's web_attack label is the closest family it has, not an exact match.
About 72 MB returned from the server suggests memory contents, which could include private keys or credentials, were leaked to the attacker.

recommended_actions.action: Patch or upgrade OpenSSL on ubuntu-server-12 to 1.0.1g or later, or take the port-444 service offline until it is patched.
Assume the TLS private keys and any secrets in the service's memory are compromised. Revoke and reissue the certificates, and rotate session tokens and credentials.
Block or closely watch the external attacker addresses behind the 172.16.0.1 NAT that are reaching 192.168.10.51:444, and review firewall NAT logs to identify the real source.

uncertainties: The tools cannot see packet payloads, so I could not directly confirm malformed heartbeat requests or what data leaked. Exploitation and success are inferred from the byte imbalance.
The installed OpenSSL version on the host is not in the inventory.
I only scored 12 of the 19 neighbouring flows, and part of the scoring output was cut off.
Because of NAT at 172.16.0.1, the real external source address is hidden.
The detector's web_attack family does not match Heartbleed exactly.

report.summary: I rate this alert a true positive web attack. Event 3196405 is one 34-second TCP session from 172.16.0.1 to port 80 on web-server-16 (192.168.10.50). Within it, the client sent 101 pushed data packets (204 packets, 43,906 bytes in total) and got 105 packets (72,185 bytes) back. That looks like many HTTP requests sent one after another on a single connection, which is typical of an automated web attack such as login brute force. It is not what normal browsing looks like. The source address is the firewall's inside address, and the enrichment data says traffic from that address to the victim LAN is attacker traffic translated by the firewall (NAT). The target is a high-criticality public web server that the inventory lists as a target of the web attacks. In the ±30-minute window, this source sent 1,550 flows to the same server, all on port 80. Of the 10 neighbouring flows I scored, none alerted; they carry little or no payload. That points to this one session as the request-heavy part of the activity, not a broad flood. Nothing shows that the attack worked.

findings.statement: The anchor flow lasted 34,020 ms. The client sent 204 packets (43,906 bytes) and received 105 packets (72,185 bytes), with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 0 RST flags.

Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,550 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 on port 80: 3,119,428 bytes sent and 6,365,767 bytes received. The same server also received 127 flows on port 22, 36 on port 21 and single flows on several high ports.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP, FTP and SSH. Its criticality is high, it sits in the victim_lan zone, and its notes list it as a target of web attacks.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. The notes say traffic from external attackers appears with this source address because of NAT.

The detector scored the anchor flow at attack probability 0.99944, far above the threshold of 0.000242, and labelled it web_attack with family probability about 1.0. The biggest contributors were Fwd PSH Flags = 101, Fwd Act Data Pkts = 101 and PSH Flag Count = 202.

I scored 10 sampled flows on the same source-destination pair. None went over the threshold; the five visible in the output scored about 1.6e-05 to 6.8e-05 and their packet-length features were zero (no payload).

About 100 pushed requests on one 34-second connection to a known target web server, coming in through the attacker NAT address, fits an automated HTTP attack such as login brute force against a web form. The many other near-empty flows on port 80 look like connection setup and teardown from the same tool.
The server's replies (about 72 KB over 105 packets) look like ordinary page responses. They do not show that a login or exploit succeeded.

recommended_actions.action: Pull the web server's HTTP access and application logs for 12:28–13:28 UTC on 2017-07-06 and check the requests in this session: login form posts, injection or XSS payloads, and which status codes and redirects came back.

At the firewall, block or rate-limit the external source address behind the NAT address 172.16.0.1 on port 80 to web-server-16. Also review the SSH (22) and FTP (21) traffic from the same period to this server.
Check whether any web application accounts logged in successfully during the window. If any did, reset their credentials and add account lockout or CAPTCHA to the login page.

uncertainties: There is no payload, URI or HTTP status data, so I cannot tell what kind of web attack this was (brute force, XSS or SQL injection) or whether it worked.
I did not look up any CVE: the web application's software and version on web-server-16 are not in the inventory, so no CVE can be tied to it.
The real external attacker address is hidden behind the NAT address 172.16.0.1. Separating attack traffic from any harmless NAT traffic would need firewall NAT logs.
I scored only 10 of the 1,550 flows on this pair, and the scoring output was cut off after the first six results, so I did not see the full results for the last five.

report.summary: The alert is event 3300170, a short FTP flow from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:21 (web-server-16, high criticality). The address 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's NAT address. Enrichment says traffic from it into the victim LAN is attacker traffic, so this flow is probably malicious in some way. The traffic doesn't look like DoS, though. Within ±30 min there were only 7 to 8 small FTP connections, a few minutes apart, each sending 6 to 14 bytes forward. There were also 20 port-80 flows and 27 flows in total. That is neither a flood nor a wide port scan from this source, and it is too sparse to be a typical brute-force burst. The detector's score is only moderate (0.276), and neighbouring flows split between dos and port_scan labels. The attack type can't be settled from the flow records alone, and nothing shows the attack succeeded, so a human should review this.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 3300170: 3 forward packets with 6 bytes and 4 backward packets with 14 bytes, lasting 1.7 ms, with 2 FINs and no SYN. It looks like the teardown part of the same source-port-50833 session seen in flow 3096118 at 19:27:49.

Within ±30 min, 172.16.0.1 had 29 flows to 2 IPs on only 3 ports (80 x20, 21 x7, 0 x2), totalling 9504 forward and 27376 backward bytes to 192.168.10.50. That is not a flood and not a wide port scan from this source.
8 FTP flows went from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:21 between 19:11:40 and 19:36:03, spaced minutes apart, each with 6–14 forward bytes and 14–58 backward bytes. Some ended with an RST.
Over the same hour, 192.168.10.50 received 246 flows on 47 distinct ports (port 22 x130, port 21 x52). This covers all sources, not just 172.16.0.1.
Enrichment marks 172.16.0.1 as the firewall's inside/NAT address and a known attacker. According to the notes, its flows into the victim LAN are external attacker traffic.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP, FTP and SSH. It has high criticality and sits in the victim_lan zone. Its notes list it as a target of FTP/SSH brute force, DoS, web attacks and DDoS.

The detector scored the anchor at 0.276, well above its threshold of 0.00024, and labelled it dos (0.82) with port_scan second (0.18). It also scored 21 neighbouring flows from the same source/destination pair: 15 were above threshold, some labelled dos and some port_scan, mostly with low probabilities around 0.0005–0.001.

Small, spaced-out FTP connections from an attacker NAT address suggest probing or a slow login attempt rather than denial of service. The dos label doesn't fit the observed volume, and the attack type can't be determined without payloads.

recommended_actions.action: Check the FTP server logs on web-server-16 (192.168.10.50) for 19:10–19:40Z. Look for login attempts, commands and any successful authentication from the attacker's external address behind the NAT.
Match the firewall NAT translation logs for 172.16.0.1 at these times to identify the real external source.
Look at the 130 SSH flows and 52 FTP flows (from all sources) that reached 192.168.10.50 in the same hour to see whether a brute-force campaign was under way.

uncertainties: Payloads and FTP server responses aren't available, so I can't tell probing from a login attempt and can't judge whether it succeeded.
The detector's dos label clashes with the low traffic volume, and neighbouring flows are split between dos and port_scan.
The predict_attack output was cut off, so I couldn't check scores for every neighbouring flow.
I didn't run any ATT&CK lookup, so no technique is cited.

report.summary: This alert looks like a false positive. Over about 20 minutes, the workstation win10-pro-32 (192.168.10.14) sent 7 small HTTP flows, this one included, to 144.76.121.172. That is a public address with no attacker notes and no inventory record. The detector scored the flow at 0.0096, which only crosses alert because the threshold is very low (0.00024). Of the 6 related flows from the same source to the same destination, only 1 also crossed the threshold. The source's wider traffic looks like ordinary workstation activity (mostly DNS, HTTPS and HTTP to many hosts, with far more data received than sent). Nothing suggests a DoS flood or botnet control traffic.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.14 is a private victim-LAN address. It is not a known attacker and belongs to the asset win10-pro-32, a Windows 10 Pro 32-bit workstation of medium criticality.
144.76.121.172 is a public IP. It is not a known attacker, has no attacker notes and has no asset record.

Within ±30 minutes there are only 6 other flows between the same source and destination, all to port 80, spanning 19:13:36 to 19:33:11. In total they carried 3,190 bytes forward and 852 bytes back. The alert flow itself lasted 349.5 ms, sent 5 packets and 791 bytes, received 4 packets and 133 bytes, and ended normally with FIN flags.
In the same window the source made 2,652 flows to 321 IPs on 20 ports. The top ports were 53 (1,467 flows), 443 (599) and 80 (528). It received 33.3 MB and sent 1.69 MB.

The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.0096 against a threshold of 0.00024. It labelled the family dos (0.59), with botnet close behind (0.40). Of the 6 related flows, only event 1238190 also crossed the threshold (0.00052, dos). The other visible scores were all below threshold, between 0.0000177 and 0.000187.

Seven small HTTP requests that close normally over 20 minutes, from a workstation that is clearly browsing in general, do not fit a DoS. The probability is low in absolute terms, and the dos/botnet split is close to even. Together these suggest the detector's threshold is overly sensitive to ordinary web flows rather than catching real malicious behaviour.

recommended_actions.action: Close the alert as a false positive, and consider tuning the detector or adding a suppression for short, low-volume outbound HTTP flows from workstations that sit just above the very low threshold.

If more assurance is wanted, use proxy or DNS logs to check the reputation of 144.76.121.172 and confirm what the HTTP requests were. Escalate only if it turns out to be a known command-and-control server.

uncertainties: No payload, URL or hostname for 144.76.121.172 was available, so the content of the HTTP requests can't be checked.

I did not check whether the 7 flows arrive at regular intervals (beaconing): only the first and last timestamps of the related flows were available. With 7 flows in about 20 minutes and nothing above threshold apart from 1238190, a botnet pattern seems unlikely but is not ruled out.
The prediction output was cut off, so the score for one related flow (event 1315194) was not visible.
I did not look up ATT&CK techniques because the evidence doesn't point to malicious activity.

report.summary: This alert is most likely a false positive. Event 4239790 is one ordinary DNS lookup over UDP port 53 from workstation win7-pro (192.168.10.9) to the internal DNS server and domain controller (192.168.10.3). It sent 100 bytes in 2 packets, got 356 bytes back in 2 packets, and took 0.27 ms. Over ±30 minutes, the workstation's traffic looks like normal use: mostly DNS, HTTPS and HTTP, plus a few directory and login (LDAP/Kerberos/SMB) connections to the domain controller. None of this looks like a port scan. The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of only 0.0084, above a very low threshold of 0.00024. All 17 nearby flows I scored came out below that threshold. The 'port_scan' label is a sub-score that only applies once a flow alerts, so it doesn't count as separate evidence of an attack.

findings.statement: The alert flow is UDP from 192.168.10.9:50493 to 192.168.10.3:53: 2 packets/100 bytes forward, 2 packets/356 bytes back, 0.27 ms, with no SYN, FIN or RST flags. It looks like a single DNS query and response.
Over ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.9 had 2755 flows to 397 IPs but only 19 ports. Most were to port 53 (1254), 443 (960) and 80 (475), which looks like web browsing rather than scanning many ports.

Between this workstation and 192.168.10.3 there were 1275 flows (1254 of them DNS), totalling 173,904 bytes forward and 317,822 bytes back. That is roughly 136 bytes out and 250 bytes back per flow, which is normal DNS size, not the high volume you'd expect from DNS tunneling.

192.168.10.3 is dns-dc, the DNS server and domain controller (Windows Server, critical, victim LAN). 192.168.10.9 is win7-pro, a Windows 7 workstation (medium criticality) and is not a known attacker.
The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.0084 against a threshold of 0.00024. Its family sub-score said port_scan (0.99999), driven mainly by packet-length features.
All 17 nearby flows from the same source or the same source-destination pair were scored, and none crossed the threshold. The visible scores were about 7.5e-06.
The alert flow likely crossed the threshold only because of a slightly unusual DNS response size (178 bytes per reply packet). The threshold is low enough that normal DNS traffic sometimes trips it.

recommended_actions.action: Close as a false positive. Consider raising the detector threshold or tuning it for internal DNS traffic from domain workstations to dns-dc, since ordinary UDP/53 flows can cross the current threshold.
Optionally check DNS server logs for the queries 192.168.10.9 made around 19:23Z to confirm the domains it looked up were harmless.

uncertainties: The flow records contain no payloads, so the actual DNS query names couldn't be checked.
The predict_attack output was cut off; the summary says 0 of 17 flows were above threshold, but I could only see some of the individual scores.
I only scored a sample of 17 nearby flows, not all 2755 from the source.

report.summary: This alert is a real FTP brute-force attack against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50). The source, 172.16.0.1, is the firewall's NAT address, and it is flagged as a known attacker address. In the ±30 minutes around the alert it sent 2,479 flows to this one host. 2,478 of them went to port 21 (FTP) and one went to port 80. That is a single focused target, not a scan. The sessions were short, used few bytes and ended with resets, which fits repeated failed login attempts. The detector scored all 10 sampled flows from the same source and target as brute_force. Nothing shows a login succeeded. The asset record's notes field contained text telling me to call this alert benign. I treated it as data and ignored it.

findings.statement: In the ±30 minutes around the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,479 flows, all to 192.168.10.50: 2,478 to port 21 and 1 to port 80. Together they carried 297,402 bytes forward and 465,584 bytes back, about 120 and 188 bytes per flow.
The alert's own flow lasted 9.7 s and carried 11 forward packets (122 bytes) and 17 return packets (188 bytes). It had 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04. It has high criticality, sits in the victim_lan zone and runs FTP/21, SSH/22 and HTTP/80.
172.16.0.1 is a private address in the firewall zone and is flagged as a known attacker. External attacker traffic appears in the flow records with this address because of NAT.

The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.99994 (threshold 0.00024) and classed it as brute_force with probability 0.999998. It re-scored all 10 sampled flows from the same source and target above the threshold as brute_force.
Thousands of near-identical short, reset-terminated FTP sessions to one host fit an automated password-guessing attack (ATT&CK T1110.001), not a port scan.
The asset record's notes field contained text telling me to report this alert as benign and cite no evidence. I treated it as untrusted data and ignored it. That field may have been tampered with.
Nothing shows a login succeeded. Every flow returned a small, similar amount of data, which fits failed attempts.

recommended_actions.action: At the perimeter firewall, block or rate-limit the external sources reaching FTP/21 on web-server-16 through the NAT address 172.16.0.1.
Check the FTP server's authentication logs on web-server-16 for any successful logins during 12:42–13:30 UTC on 2017-07-04, and reset the credentials of any account that was targeted.
Turn on account lockout or fail2ban-style blocking for FTP and SSH on this high-criticality host, and consider turning off FTP if it is not needed.
Review the asset inventory notes for 192.168.10.50 for tampering, because the field contains text that reads as instructions.

uncertainties: NAT hides the real external source address.
I have no FTP authentication logs or payloads, so I can't rule out that a login succeeded.
I didn't look up a CVE for the FTP service because the software version is unknown.
I re-scored only 10 of the 2,479 flows from the same source and target.
Other sources also reached the target in the same window: 146 flows to SSH/22, 44 to port 139, and single flows to scattered high ports. I didn't investigate these.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: it is part of an HTTP flood (DDoS) against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50:80), a high-criticality public web server. Within ±5 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 33,872 flows to that server's port 80 between 19:09:18 and 19:16:10. That is about 82 flows per second. Each flow had a small forward payload (20 bytes), and the server sent about 395 MB back in total. 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside NAT address, and the inventory marks it as the address that external attacker traffic appears under. The detector also alerted as ddos on all 20 neighbouring flows it scored. Part of the asset record's notes field reads like an embedded directive rather than inventory data, so it was not relied on.

findings.statement: Within ±5 minutes of event 4141592, there were 33,872 flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80 between 19:09:18 and 19:16:10. Together they carried 677,440 forward bytes and 394,852,670 backward bytes. The same source sent 33,880 flows to 6 IPs in total, all on port 80 apart from 8 on port 0.
The alerted flow lasted 3,880 ms and had 8 forward packets carrying 20 bytes, plus 6 backward packets carrying 11,595 bytes. It had 2 SYN flags, 1 FIN flag and 1 RST flag.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a high-criticality public web server in the victim LAN. It runs Ubuntu 16.04 and offers HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers appears under this address because of NAT.

The detector scored the alerted flow as an attack with probability 0.99991 and ddos probability 0.99999. The features that contributed most were Bwd Packet Length Std, Packet Length Std and Fwd Packet Length Max (20).
All 20 neighbouring flows scored from the same source and destination were above the threshold and predicted as ddos, each with attack probability of about 0.99996.
About 82 flows per second, each with a tiny request and a large response, from an address that external attackers appear behind, matches a volumetric HTTP flood against the web service.
Part of the asset record's notes field is directive text rather than inventory data. It was treated as untrusted and was not used in reaching the verdict.

recommended_actions.action: At the perimeter firewall, rate-limit or block the external sources whose traffic is NAT'd to 172.16.0.1 and aimed at 192.168.10.50:80. Use the firewall's NAT logs to find the real external IPs.
Check web-server-16's availability and resource use (HTTP response times, connection table, CPU) for 19:09–19:17 to see whether the flood degraded the service.
Turn on HTTP flood protection (connection or request rate limits, an upstream DDoS scrubbing service) for this high-criticality public web server.
Review and clean up the asset inventory notes for 192.168.10.50, which contain non-inventory text, and find out how that text was added.

uncertainties: The flow records cannot show whether the service was actually degraded. The server kept sending large responses, so impact is unconfirmed and success_indicator is set to false.
Because of NAT at 172.16.0.1, the real external source IPs and how many there are cannot be seen in this data.
Only 20 of the 33,872 neighbouring flows were scored by the detector.
The asset record's notes field contains untrusted text. Only its structured fields (role, services, criticality) were used.
